# MapMaker lessons on the Support Hub (questions, layers and sources)
Built 2026-10-22 from the lesson files by the MapMaker resource pages, Vera knowledge builder 1.6. Do not edit by hand; edit the lesson files and rebuild.

How to use this file: each lesson below has its own MapMaker map. When a teacher names one of these lessons (by title or lesson ID) and asks for new or different questions, base every question only on the bookmarks, layers and pop-up content listed for that lesson, and use bookmark and layer names exactly as written. If a request needs information that lesson's map does not show, say so plainly instead of inventing it. Use only the links listed for that lesson. The answers to the lessons' questions are not in this file: do not give them, and do not write student material that contains them.

### 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles
**Lesson ID:** revolutionary-battles-1775-1776
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Road to revolution and the Revolution. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=bda07736a1b9425ea19fdde282088bd6)
**Description:** Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Social Studies.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Locate the 21 battles of 1775–1776 on the map and sort them by year, using the pop-up dates and the legend for the winner.
- Measure straight-line distances between Boston, Concord, New York, Philadelphia and Trenton with the Measure tool.
- Identify the major ports between Boston and Charleston from the Key Port Cities layer and the coastline, and explain what a navy based at New York could reach.
- Trace the end of 1776 through the numbered Turning Points and the Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton pop-ups.
- Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the fighting moved from Boston to New York and across New Jersey.
**Bookmarks in this map:** Massachusetts.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Revolutionary War Battles: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates, a picture and a short account. The winner is shown only by the diamond's color, as listed in the legend (American Victory or British Victory); the pop-up does not state it in words; source: American Battlefield Trust.
- Revolutionary War Battlefields: Battlefield boundaries (gray) and the core areas where the fighting was heaviest (diagonal stripes). No pop-ups; source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Turning Points: Five white circles numbered 1 to 5, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, that appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the event's name, year, a short account (the Battle_details field) and the victor; source: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources.
- Thirteen British Colonies: Colony areas and borders in 1763. The pop-up gives the colony's name; source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988).
- 1763 Proclamation Line: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlement; source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988).
- Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens): Ports that supplied armies and moved troops, from New England to the Caribbean and Britain. The legend separates a Major Port City (larger symbol) from a smaller Port. The layer has no pop-ups and no labels; source: Jay Feyerabend, [master's thesis](https://commons.lib.jmu.edu/masters202029/74), James Madison University (2021).
**What students read before they start:** British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Diamonds mark battles. A battle's pop-up gives its name, dates and story, but not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner, so use the legend. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened. The Key Port Cities layer has no pop-ups: the legend tells a major port from a smaller one.
**Compelling question:** Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Where did the war begin? On the map: Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord and read its dates. Open the legend and check which color shows who won. Click the Boston diamond and read its dates. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord. Answer: When was Lexington and Concord fought, and who won? How long did the siege of Boston last? Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: ________ miles
2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? On the map: Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each diamond and write its name under the year it was fought. Use the legend to mark who won each battle. Answer: Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
3. Why New York? On the map: In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (inside Revolutionary War Battlefields). Use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port. Find the major ports between Boston and Charleston. The layer has no pop-ups, so use the coastline and the battle diamonds nearby to name them. Use Measure from New York to Philadelphia and from New York to Boston. Answer: Boston and Charleston are major ports: which other major ports lie between them? Looking at the map, what could a navy based at New York reach? New York to Philadelphia: ________ miles. New York to Boston: ________ miles
4. How did 1776 end? On the map: Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear. Follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. Read each one's dates, and use the legend to see who won. Use Measure for the distance from New York City to Trenton. Answer: When was each battle fought, and who won? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: ________ miles
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about 1775–1776 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** siege, militia, Continental Army, Loyalist, harbor, campaign, retreat.
**Standards:** TX 8.4(C); TX 8.10(A); TX 8.10(C); FL SS.8.A.3.6; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.8.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### Roads, Trails, and Rails West
**Lesson ID:** roads-trails-and-rails-west
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Roads, Trails, and Rails West in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=3ec83a9d66454ade8aead0a64872d931)
**Description:** Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Indigenous Studies, Economics.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Identify where three of the seven trails started and ended from their pop-ups, and explain from the map why most began in Missouri.
- Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the Oregon Trail's length in its pop-up.
- Name Indigenous nations whose lands a trail crossed, using the Indigenous Territories layer.
- Compare the transcontinental railroad lines in the legend with the dotted trails to see which routes the railroads followed.
- Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how trails and then railroads changed the West, and for whom.
**Bookmarks in this map:** none.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Trails West: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each a dotted line in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up is titled with the trail's name and gives a short history with places, dates and distances; source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information.
- Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911 (off when the map opens): Five transcontinental lines as thick colored lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific), Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) and Southern Pacific. No pop-up. In the Railroads group; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Railroads 1826 to 1911 (off when the map opens): All railroad lines built from 1826 to 1911, as thin gray lines. Each pop-up gives the railroad's name (where recorded) and the year it was in operation by. In the Railroads group; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Indigenous Territories (off when the map opens): Approximate territories of Indigenous nations, from a community-made map, each shaded in its own color with the nation's name appearing when zoomed in. Not listed in the legend. No pop-up; source: Native Land Digital.
**What students read before they start:** In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them, and clicking a trail opens its pop-up. City and state names are part of the basemap. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, named in the legend, and thin gray lines are other railroads; only the thin gray lines have pop-ups. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color, and its name appears when you zoom in. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.
**Compelling question:** How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Where did the trails begin? On the map: Open the legend to see which color is which trail. Click three of the dotted trail lines. Read in each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Answer: Where did each trail start and end? In which state do most of the trails start?
2. How far, and how many? On the map: Find the Oregon Trail's color in the legend. Click the Oregon Trail and read its length and how many people traveled it. Find Independence, Missouri, on the basemap, next to Kansas City. Use Measure for a straight line from Independence to Portland, Oregon. Answer: How long was the Oregon Trail, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: ________ miles
3. Whose land? On the map: In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories. Zoom in until the nations' names appear. Follow one trail from one end to the other. Find two nations whose land it crossed. Answer: Which two nations' land did the trail cross? Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
4. From trails to rails On the map: In Map layers, turn on Railroads. Use the legend to find the Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines. Click a thin gray railroad line and read when it was in operation by. Answer: Which trails do the Transcontinental Railroad lines follow most closely? By when was the gray railroad line in operation?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about the journey west that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** Manifest Destiny, emigrant, trail, transcontinental railroad, telegraph, Indigenous nation.
**Standards:** TX 8.6(B); TX 8.6(C); TX 8.11(A); FL SS.8.A.4.1; C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.7.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850
**Lesson ID:** us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Reform and the road to war. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=819f60a5a3344d958d24f505849abaaa)
**Description:** Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Civics, Social Studies.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the legend to tell free states and slave states apart, including those set by compromise, and locate the eastern line between them.
- Read the year each state became free or slave from its pop-up, and the year of the Missouri Compromise Line from its pop-up.
- Explain why Missouri, a slave state lying mostly north of the Missouri Compromise Line, was an exception.
- Trace the internal slave-trade routes from Virginia to the Gulf coast and the Underground Railroad routes north to the Great Lakes and Canada, naming states and towns from the map.
- Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how slavery divided the United States by 1850.
**Bookmarks in this map:** Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- US States and Territories 1850: States and territories in four legend groups: Free states; Free states and territories by compromise; Slave states; and Slave states and territories by compromise. Each pop-up is titled with the state's name and says whether it allowed slavery and from what year; source: Traced from a map in Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), as the pop-ups say.
- Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade: Solid black lines along which enslaved people were forced to move within the United States, with no arrows; dashed and dotted lines in the same layer are sea routes and the voyages of the Amistad and the Creole. No pop-up; source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920).
- Underground Railroad Approximate Routes: Approximate routes that freedom seekers took north to the free states and Canada, as orange lines. No pop-up; source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), an early-1900s interpretation.
- Cities: 69 towns and cities along the Underground Railroad routes, from Virginia and Kentucky to Ontario and Quebec, as dots with name labels that appear when zoomed in. No pop-up; source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920).
- Missouri Compromise Line: The line at 36°30′ North set in 1820. Its pop-up gives the line's name, the year it was enacted and a note on what it divided; source: Not stated on the layer (hosted by the MapMaker team).
- US 1850 Original Map (off when the map opens): A scan of the 1850 map that the other layers were traced from. No pop-up; source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920).
**What students read before they start:** By 1850, the Northern states had ended slavery or passed laws to end it, but in the South slavery was legal and growing. More than 3 million people were enslaved in the United States. Each time a new state joined the Union, Congress argued over whether slavery would be allowed there.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** States and territories are shaded brown if they were free and green if they allowed slavery; the paler shades mean free, or slave, because of a compromise. Open the legend to see the four groups. Click a state to read its name and year in the pop-up. A gray dashed line marks the Missouri Compromise Line; click it for its pop-up. Solid black lines are internal routes of the slave trade. They have no arrows. Dashed and dotted lines in the same layer show sea routes and the voyages of two ships, the Amistad and the Creole. Orange lines are approximate Underground Railroad routes. Zoom in to see the towns along them: orange dots in the United States, black dots in Canada.
**Compelling question:** How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Free states and slave states On the map: Open the legend and find the four groups for US States and Territories 1850. Click a state in each group to read its name. Click two states to read what year each became free or slave. Answer: Which groups are free and which allow slavery? Where is the line between free and slave states in the East?
2. The Missouri Compromise On the map: Find the Missouri Compromise Line (the gray dashed line). Click it and read its pop-up. Find the slave state that lies mostly north of the line. Answer: What year was the Missouri Compromise enacted? Slavery was banned north of the line in the Louisiana Territory: which slave state lies mostly north of it, and why does that matter?
3. The internal slave trade On the map: In Map layers, turn off Underground Railroad Approximate Routes so the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade stand out. Click the states where the lines begin and read their names. Click the states where the lines come together and read their names. Find where the lines reach the coast. Answer: Where do the lines reach the coast? The lines have no arrows: from the pattern and what you have learned, which way were enslaved people forced to move?
4. Routes to freedom On the map: Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark. Follow the orange Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River. Zoom in to read the names of the towns along them. Answer: Where do the routes lead? Why do you think many keep going past the free states?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about slavery in 1850 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** free state, slave state, Missouri Compromise, Fugitive Slave Act, Underground Railroad, freedom seeker, abolition.
**Standards:** FL SS.8.A.5.2; TX 8.10(A); C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.8.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### Civil War Battlefields
**Lesson ID:** civil-war-battlefields
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The Civil War. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Civil War Battlefields in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=7a06e8e2818941f99a3d40bb32e08118)
**Description:** See how the United States was divided by 1863, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Civics, Economics.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Sort the states on the 1863 map into those that seceded before Fort Sumter, those that seceded after, and the slave states that stayed in the Union, using the legend, and notice that the layer shows 1863, so West Virginia appears as a Union state that did not exist in 1861.
- Locate Washington, D.C., identify the two states that border it, and explain from their legend shades why Maryland staying in the Union mattered.
- Compare the density of railroads north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy and say why that difference mattered in a war.
- Find battlefields in Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania, read their names and sizes from the pop-ups, and identify which were fought in Union states.
- Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how the geography of a divided nation shaped the Civil War.
**Bookmarks in this map:** none.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863): States and territories in 1863 in five legend groups: Union free states; Union slave states (border states); slave states that seceded before Fort Sumter, April 1861; slave states that seceded after Fort Sumter; and territories. State names are labeled on the map. No pop-up; source: State boundaries from IPUMS NHGIS, grouped by the MapMaker team.
- Civil War Battlefield Boundary: The land each battle covered, as tan shaded areas. Each pop-up gives the battle's name, its size in acres and the state (two-letter code); source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Civil War Core Areas: The core of each battlefield, where the heaviest fighting took place, as striped areas. Same pop-up as the boundaries; source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Boundary between Union and Confederacy: The line between the Union and the Confederacy. No pop-up; source: Not stated on the layer (hosted by the MapMaker team).
- Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static): Railroads built by 1863. No pop-up; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Civil War Battlefields: Battle locations as diamonds colored by result (Union victory, Confederate victory, Inconclusive) and sized by casualties; gray circles are battles with no result recorded (Other). Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates and a picture; it does not give the result. The diamonds disappear when you zoom in very close; source: American Battlefield Trust.
**What students read before they start:** In November 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. He opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories, and Southern slave states began to leave the Union to form the Confederate States of America. In April 1861, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, a Union fort in South Carolina, and the Civil War began.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** States are shaded by side in 1863: shades of blue for the Union and shades of brown for the Confederacy; open the legend to see which shade means which group. State names are written on the map. A white dashed line marks the boundary between the two sides. Thin dark gray lines are railroads built by 1863. Diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result. White diamonds are Inconclusive and gray circles are Other. Bigger diamonds mean more soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or missing. Tan shaded areas show the land each battlefield covered, and areas with diagonal stripes show where the fighting was heaviest.
**Compelling question:** How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War, as the map shows the country in 1863?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. A nation divided On the map: Open the legend and find the groups for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863). Match each state's shade to its group. Find the state on the map that did not exist in 1861 (the layer shows the country in 1863). Answer: Which states left the Union before the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861? Which left after? Which slave states stayed in the Union? Which state on the map did not exist in 1861?
2. The border states On the map: Zoom in to Washington, D.C., on the east coast between Maryland and Virginia. Find the two states that border it. Check each one's shade in the legend. Answer: Which two states border Washington, D.C.? What would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?
3. Railroads, North and South On the map: Find the white dashed boundary between the Union and the Confederacy. In Map layers, turn U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) off to see the railroad lines better. Compare the railroads (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the boundary. Answer: Which side had more railroads? Why would railroads matter in a war?
4. Where were the battles? On the map: Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania. Click the tan shaded areas of two battlefields and read their names. Use the legend to find a battlefield in a Union state. Answer: Where were most battles fought? Name a battle fought in a state the legend shows as a Union state.
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about the Civil War that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** secession, Union, Confederacy, border state, Fort Sumter, battlefield, railroad network.
**Standards:** FL SS.8.A.5.4; TX 8.10(A); TX 8.10(C); C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.7.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### The Battle of Vicksburg
**Lesson ID:** the-battle-of-vicksburg
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The Civil War. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The Battle of Vicksburg in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=1ba8cd3fc75a49a497be1137fce4c032)
**Description:** Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Social Studies.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Locate Vicksburg on the Mississippi River and follow the railroad east to Jackson to explain why both sides wanted the city.
- Put the key places on Grant's route in order, say which bank of the river each is on, and measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.
- List the battles of the Vicksburg campaign in date order from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups.
- Identify from the basemap which Confederate states lay west of the Mississippi and what the Union controlled once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had fallen.
- Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the Union needed Vicksburg and how Grant took it.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The Battle of Vicksburg.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg: Places on Grant's route in spring 1863, as dark pins labeled on the map: Miliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards, plus a yellow pin at Vicksburg. No pop-ups; source: Placed by the MapMaker team.
- Railroads 1826 to 1911: Railroads built from 1826 to 1911, so it includes lines built after the war. They only draw when zoomed in. No pop-up; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Civil War Battlefields (off when the map opens): Civil War battles as diamonds colored by result. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates and a picture; it does not give the result; source: American Battlefield Trust.
**What students read before they start:** In 1862, Union forces captured New Orleans and Memphis, two cities on the Mississippi River. Between the two, the Confederates still held part of the river, including the city of Vicksburg, Mississippi. In spring 1863, Union General Ulysses S. Grant set out to capture it.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The yellow pin is Vicksburg. Dark pins mark places on Grant's route, each with its name. City and state names, such as Jackson and Louisiana, are part of the basemap. Railroads are thin dark lines with short cross marks, like a track; they appear when you zoom in, and they include lines built after the war. Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers. Its diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result.
**Compelling question:** Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Why Vicksburg? On the map: Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Find Vicksburg, the yellow pin on the Mississippi River. Zoom in until the railroads appear and follow the line east from Vicksburg. Find Jackson, Mississippi, on the basemap (the state capital, east of Vicksburg). Answer: Why would both sides want Vicksburg?
2. Grant's route On the map: Find the dark pins for Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards. Check which side of the river each pin is on. Use Measure for the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend. Answer: Which side of the river is each place on? Why did Grant march south before crossing the river? Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend: ________ miles
3. The battles of May 1863 On the map: In Map layers, turn on Civil War Battlefields. Click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg and read their dates. Click the diamonds east toward Jackson and read their dates. Answer: Which battles were fought between Bruinsburg Bend, Vicksburg and Jackson? List them in order by date.
4. Splitting the Confederacy On the map: Zoom out until you can see the Mississippi River from Memphis to the Gulf of Mexico. Keep Civil War Battlefields on and click the diamond at Port Hudson, in Louisiana south of Vicksburg. Read when the siege of Port Hudson ended. Read the state names on the basemap. Answer: When did Port Hudson end? Which states lie west of the river? What could the Union control once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had both fallen?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about the Vicksburg campaign that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** siege, campaign, bluff, gunboat, supply line, surrender.
**Standards:** FL SS.8.A.5.1; TX 8.10(C); C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.7.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791
**Lesson ID:** we-the-people-1787-1791
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Confederation and the Constitution. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=eba1ea7488624f3c88ef094167ed03ca)
**Description:** See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.
**Subjects:** US History, Civics, Government, Data Literacy.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Compare the pie sizes in the Population in 1790 layer to find the most populous state, and read the census line of the pop-ups to identify the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.
- Use the labels and legend of the House seats in 1793 layer to find the states with the most and fewest House seats, and compare each state's House seats with its two senators.
- Read the Virginia and South Carolina pop-ups to compare the seats each actually had with the seats it would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all.
- Read the vote line in the Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups to find the three closest ratification votes and explain why North Carolina has two pies.
- Use population and seat figures from at least two states as evidence for how the three-fifths clause shifted power in the House.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The states in 1790; New England and New York; The South.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Population in 1790: free and enslaved: A pie on each state: free people (blue) and enslaved people (orange-red) in the 1790 census, with bigger pies for more people. Each pop-up, titled with the state's name, gives the total, the number enslaved and the percentage, the number counted under the three-fifths clause, the state's House seats in 1793, its two senators, and the seats it would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all; source: U.S. Census Bureau, 1790 census and apportionment ratio; Apportionment Act of April 14, 1792 (National Archives); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- House seats in 1793 (off when the map opens): States shaded from pale to dark blue by their House seats under the apportionment act of 14 April 1792 (legend: 1 to 2, 4 to 6, 7 to 10, 13 to 19 seats), labeled with the state's abbreviation and seats. Same pop-up as the population layer; source: National Archives.
- House seats today (2020 apportionment) (off when the map opens): Each state's House seats after the 2020 census; source: U.S. Census Bureau (MapMaker catalogue).
- Ratifying the Constitution, 1787–1791 (off when the map opens): A pie where each state's ratifying convention met: votes to ratify (blue) and against (orange-red), with bigger pies for more delegates. Labels give the state and the order it ratified (DE 1 to VT 14). Each pop-up gives the result, date and vote, where the convention met, and a note. North Carolina has two pies: its first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788 (label NC (1788)), did not ratify; source: Center for the Study of the American Constitution, University of Wisconsin–Madison (votes, dates and meeting places).
**What students read before they start:** In 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution. Large and small states disagreed about how many votes each should have in Congress. The Constitution would take effect only when nine states had ratified it, each at a special convention.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click a pie or a state to see its name in the pop-up title. Pies on the states show the people in 1790: blue for free, orange-red for enslaved, and bigger pies for more people. Three layers are off when the map opens. In House seats in 1793, darker blue means more seats, and each label gives the state's abbreviation and seats. In Ratifying the Constitution, each pie sits where a state's convention met: blue for votes to ratify, orange-red for votes against, and labels give the order each state ratified. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia.
**Compelling question:** How did the Constitution balance large and small states, and how close did it come to being rejected?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Who lived where in 1790? On the map: Open The states in 1790 bookmark. Click the pies and read each pop-up. Read the first line of each pop-up, which gives the percentage enslaved. Answer: Which state had the most people? In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved?
2. Seats in Congress On the map: In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793. Read the labels: each gives the state and its seats, and darker blue means more seats. Click two states and read how many senators each had. Answer: Which state had the most seats in the House of Representatives, and which the fewest? How many senators did each of your two states have? Why do you think the House and the Senate are counted differently?
3. The three-fifths clause On the map: Click Virginia and South Carolina. Read the last two lines of each pop-up: seats with enslaved people counted in full, or not at all. Click other states and read the same two lines. Answer: Under the three-fifths clause, three of every five enslaved people were counted when House seats were shared out. How many seats would Virginia and South Carolina each have had if enslaved people had been counted in full, or not at all? Which states gained seats by counting people who could not vote? Virginia: ____ seats with the three-fifths clause; ____ if enslaved people were not counted.
4. How close was ratification? On the map: In Map layers, turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793. Turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Click the pies and read the first line of each pop-up: the votes for and against. Find North Carolina and click both of its pies. Answer: Which three votes were closest? Why does North Carolina have two pies?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about the Constitution that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** ratify, convention, census, apportionment, Great Compromise, three-fifths clause, Federalist, Anti-Federalist.
**Standards:** TX 8.4(D); TX 8.17(A); FL SS.8.A.3.10; FL SS.8.A.3.11; C3 D2.Civ.5.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.6.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live
**Lesson ID:** rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Confederation and the Constitution. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=59467ac7d7c64542acaa6a3e9c19ebf4)
**Description:** Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.
**Subjects:** US History, Civics, Government, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Zoom to their own town, click inside their congressional district to read the representative's name, party and district number, and count the districts in their state.
- Use the Topographic basemap labels to find four public places in their community and sketch a labelled pin on each with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.
- Add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens, and sort those responsibilities into required by law and voluntary.
- Turn on the National Register of Historic Places layer, identify the two listed places nearest the school using the pop-up address and the basemap, and connect one public building to a right or responsibility.
- Use the places they pinned as evidence to explain where in their community rights and responsibilities are exercised.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The United States.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Congressional districts (119th Congress): District boundaries for the 119th Congress (2025–2027) as blue outlines, current as of the layer's last update (see its item page); representatives change at elections and in special elections. Each pop-up reads "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]"; source: Esri; U.S. Census Bureau; Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives (MapMaker catalogue).
- National Register of Historic Places (off when the map opens): Places on the National Register as diamonds colored by type: building, structure, district, site or object. They appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the address, city, county and state, and a link to the National Archives record, but not the place's name; read the name from the basemap label or the National Archives record; source: National Park Service (MapMaker catalogue).
**What students read before they start:** In 1791, ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added to the Constitution. They protect rights such as freedom of speech, religion and the press, the right to gather peacefully, and the right to a fair trial. Citizens also have responsibilities to their community and their country.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The Topographic basemap has place names, and labels public buildings when you zoom in close. Blue lines are the boundaries of congressional districts for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); click inside one to see who represents it. National Register of Historic Places is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers and zoom in to see its diamonds, colored by type of place (see the legend). Its pop-ups give an address but not a name. Put your pins on public places, not homes. Sketches are not saved when you close the map.
**Compelling question:** Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Who represents us? On the map: Zoom to your town; the basemap has place names. Find the blue lines, which are the boundaries of congressional districts. Click inside your district and read the pop-up. Zoom out to see your whole state. Answer: Who represents your district in the House of Representatives, which party do they belong to, and what is the district's number? How many districts does your state have?
2. Rights in public places On the map: Zoom in on your town until the basemap shows building names. Find four public places, not homes: a courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office. Use Sketch to put a pin on each one. Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Finish in one lesson or take a screenshot, because sketches are not saved. Answer: Which four places did you pin, and which right from the Bill of Rights do people use at each?
3. Responsibilities On the map: Start at the courthouse or city hall you pinned. Add a pin at each place where people carry out a citizen's responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes. Next to each pin, write the responsibility. Answer: Which of these responsibilities are required by law, and which are voluntary?
4. History where we live On the map: In Map layers, turn on National Register of Historic Places. Zoom in until the diamonds appear and click the two nearest your school; the pop-up gives the address. Read the name from the basemap label under the diamond or the pop-up's National Archive Information link. Use the legend to tell a building from a district or a site. Answer: Is either a public building, such as a courthouse, post office, school or library? Which right or responsibility does it connect with?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about your own community that you hadn't noticed before?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** amendment, Bill of Rights, civil liberties, citizen, responsibility, congressional district, representative, jury.
**Standards:** TX 8.19(B); TX 8.19(C); FL SS.8.CG.2.5; C3 D2.Civ.2.6-8; C3 D2.Civ.8.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.6.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### Political Parties and Federal Power, 1796–1819
**Lesson ID:** presidential-elections-1796-1800
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The early republic. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Political Parties and Federal Power, 1796–1819 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=6173219d9cd84812bcd4fed859b2c182)
**Description:** Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and find two Supreme Court cases that shaped the new government. The elections of 1796 and 1800 show the first party divide; two Supreme Court cases, in 1803 and 1819, show how the new federal government's power was tested.
**Subjects:** US History, Government, Civics, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 layer to describe which regions voted mostly for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the split states for their numbers.
- Switch between the 1796 and 1800 layers to find the state whose whole pie changed color and the states whose shares changed.
- Read the two-color pies in the Election of 1800 layer to identify the closest state.
- Click the two Supreme Court case markers, read what happened in each place, and measure the straight-line distance between them.
- Use the pattern of electors' votes across the sixteen states as evidence to describe where each party was strong in 1800.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The sixteen states.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Election of 1796: electors' votes: A pie on each of the 16 states: electors' votes for John Adams (Federalist, orange) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican, blue), with bigger pies for more electors. Each pop-up lists the votes for each main candidate, with the rest grouped as others; source: National Archives (Electoral College results); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- Election of 1800: electors' votes (off when the map opens): The same for 1800. Each pop-up lists every candidate's votes and explains the Jefferson–Burr tie and the 12th Amendment, so no question asks for those; source: National Archives (Electoral College results); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819: Pink squares for Marbury v. Madison (1803, Washington, D.C.) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819, Baltimore), labeled with the case name and year. Each pop-up gives the question, the ruling, why it matters and why it's placed there (Why here); source: National Archives (Milestone Documents).
**What students read before they start:** George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name and its number of electors. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); use the legend. Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases; each pop-up has a Why here part. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia, and territories aren't shown.
**Compelling question:** How did the first political parties divide the country?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. The election of 1796 On the map: Open The sixteen states bookmark. Use the legend to read the 1796 pies. Click each two-color pie and read its pop-up. Answer: Which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson? Which states split their votes, and how?
2. The election of 1800 On the map: In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Find the two-color pies. Click each one and read how its electors divided. Answer: Which states have two-color pies this time? How did each one's electors divide between Adams and Jefferson? Which state was the closest?
3. Which states switched? On the map: In Map layers, switch between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 (one on, one off). Find the state whose whole pie changed from orange to blue, and click it to read its electors. Find the states whose pies changed their shares, and check New England. Answer: Which state's whole pie changed from orange to blue, and how many electors did it have? Which states' pies changed their shares, and did any New England state change? Using both maps, where was each party strong and where did the two parties compete? Changed completely: ____________, with ____ electors.
4. The Supreme Court, near the capital On the map: Click the two pink squares: Marbury v. Madison (1803) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). Read the Why here part of each pop-up. Use Measure to find the straight-line distance between the two squares. Answer: What happened in each place to bring the case to the Court? How far apart are the two squares? Why might both cases have come from so near the national capital? Distance between the two cases: about ____ miles.
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about the first political parties that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** political party, Federalist, Democratic-Republican, elector, Electoral College, 12th Amendment, judicial review, implied powers.
**Standards:** TX 8.5(D); TX 8.18(A); TX 8.18(B); FL SS.8.A.3.13; FL SS.8.A.3.14; C3 D2.Civ.4.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.7.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806
**Lesson ID:** louisiana-purchase-1803-1806
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The early republic. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=f8af7269e5c14e69b060d6184d04ff85)
**Description:** Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Indigenous Studies, Economics.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the legend to compare the Louisiana Purchase with the land of 1783 and read the purchase pop-up for its size and price.
- Use the United States Watersheds layer to name the Ohio and Missouri watersheds and trace on the basemap where their rivers reach the sea.
- Follow the Lewis and Clark trail and campsites up the Missouri and use the Biomes layer to name the biomes the expedition crossed.
- Find where the trail leaves the Louisiana Purchase and measure the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific coast.
- Use the watershed boundaries and river routes as evidence to explain why New Orleans mattered to farmers west of the Appalachians.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The Louisiana Purchase; Up the Missouri; Across the Rockies to the Pacific.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Territorial acquisitions to 1803: The land Britain gave up in 1783 (green) and the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 (yellow). Edges of the purchase that were settled later are in other colors or stripes: with Britain in 1818, and with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848. Each pop-up gives a short note; source: MapMaker catalogue (US territorial acquisitions).
- Biomes (off when the map opens): Today's biomes, shaded by type; each pop-up names the biome (first line), the realm and the ecoregion (a modern reference layer, not a historical reconstruction); source: RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017, via Esri (MapMaker catalogue).
- United States Watersheds (off when the map opens): River basins outlined in brown, from the 22 largest regions (Hydrologic Unit Code 2s, such as Ohio Region and Missouri Region) down to small watersheds as you zoom in; each pop-up names the basin and lists the states it touches (a modern reference layer, not a historical reconstruction); source: U.S. Geological Survey Watershed Boundary Dataset, via Esri (MapMaker catalogue).
- Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail: The National Park Service's line of the expedition's route, about 4,900 miles from Pittsburgh to the mouth of the Columbia River. No pop-up: the line has no information to click; source: National Park Service, Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail.
- Lewis and Clark campsites (approximate): Approximate places where the Corps of Discovery camped, 1803–1806. No pop-up: the symbols have no information to click; source: National Park Service, from Robert Bergantino, Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology.
**What students read before they start:** In 1803 the United States bought France's claim to a huge area west of the Mississippi River. Native nations lived on and governed most of that land; the National Park Service says the expedition met more than 50 Tribal Nations. President Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to explore it and look for a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The expedition set out in 1803 and returned in 1806.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click an area to see its name. Use the legend: green is the land Britain gave up to the United States in 1783; yellow is the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Edges of the purchase settled later have other colors or stripes. A purple line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, and small symbols mark the Corps' approximate campsites; the line and the symbols have no pop-ups. United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens and show today's landscape. Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.
**Compelling question:** What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. A bigger country On the map: Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark and use the legend. Compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of the United States in 1783. Click the Louisiana Purchase and read its pop-up. Answer: About how much bigger did the country become? How much land was the Louisiana Purchase, and what did it cost? Size: about ____ million acres. Price: $____ million.
2. Why New Orleans? On the map: In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio River and the Missouri River. Zoom out and follow the rivers on the map to where they end. Answer: Which river regions are the two outlines? Into which big river do they flow, and which city sits near its mouth? In 1800 farmers west of the Appalachians sent their crops to market by river: why did control of New Orleans matter to them?
3. Up the Missouri On the map: Open the Up the Missouri bookmark. Follow the trail line and the campsite symbols up the Missouri River. In Map layers, turn off United States Watersheds and turn on Biomes. Click the shading along the route and read the first line of the pop-up. Look at where the campsites sit. Answer: Which biome covers the Great Plains? Why do you think the Corps traveled along rivers?
4. Across the Rockies On the map: Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Find where the trail line leaves the yellow Louisiana Purchase. Zoom out and find the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where the Ohio River begins. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the trail's western end on the Pacific coast. Answer: Where does the trail line leave the Louisiana Purchase? Was the Pacific coast part of it? What is the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific end of the trail? Straight-line distance: ________ miles. The trail itself is about 4,900 miles long.
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** The United States bought this land from France. Before you start says the Corps of Discovery met more than 50 Tribal Nations along the way. Whose land was it, and what does the map leave out?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** Louisiana Purchase, Corps of Discovery, expedition, watershed, river basin, biome, Continental Divide, Tribal Nation.
**Standards:** TX 8.6(B); TX 8.10(A); TX 8.10(C); FL SS.8.A.3.14; FL SS.8.G.1.2; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.7.1, updated 2026-10-22.

### The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823
**Lesson ID:** war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The early republic. **Time:** 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=fad1cdb9d5704401a4e05c34f7ee693c)
**Description:** Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Government.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the battle diamonds in the Battles of the War of 1812 layer to identify the three main areas of fighting.
- Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.
- Read the pop-ups of the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line layers to describe what the treaty settled.
- Compare the dates of independence and US recognition in the Latin American independence layer with Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
- Use the locations of the battles and the 1819 boundary as evidence to explain how the United States' position in North America changed between 1812 and 1823.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The War of 1812; The 1819 boundary; Latin America in 1825.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Historic National Boundaries: 1800: Borders in 1800, before the Louisiana Purchase, with the United States shaded pink. Each pop-up names the country; source: University of Minnesota (historic national boundaries), from the MapMaker catalogue.
- Land Spain gave up in 1819 (off when the map opens): Land Spain gave up in the Adams–Onís Treaty, including East and West Florida (green). Each pop-up gives a short note; source: MapMaker catalogue (US territorial acquisitions).
- Battlefield Boundaries: War of 1812: The land each battlefield covered (tan) and its core area (lighter tan). Each pop-up gives the battle and its size in acres; source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 (off when the map opens): The 1819 boundary with Spain as a pink dashed line in seven parts, drawn from the treaty's description and approximate. Each pop-up describes its part; source: Treaty text from the Avalon Project, Yale Law School; drawn on Natural Earth rivers.
- Battles of the War of 1812: 52 battles from 1811 to 1815 as diamonds: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if inconclusive; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. Each pop-up gives the dates, the victor, total casualties, a casualties chart, the leaders on each side and a short account. The legend labels every opponent of the United States as British, but some battles were fought against Native nations: Tippecanoe (the Shawnee-led confederacy), Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend (Red Stick Creeks). The pop-up's leaders and story say who fought; source: American Battlefield Trust (War of 1812 Battles map).
- Latin American independence and US recognition (off when the map opens): Ten Latin American nations, labeled with the year of independence: blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824, orange diamonds if it recognized them later (1826 to 1862). Each pop-up gives the capital, today's countries, independence and recognition; source: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State; Library of Congress country studies.
**What students read before they start:** In the early 1800s Britain and France were at war, and both seized American ships. British warships also forced sailors off American ships into the Royal Navy, and Britain supported Native nations resisting American settlement. In June 1812 the United States declared war on Britain.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows the United States in 1800. Diamonds mark battles; use the legend: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if neither side won; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. The legend says British for every opponent, but some battles were fought against Native nations: the pop-up's leaders and story tell you who fought. Each battle pop-up gives the dates, the victor and the casualties. Tan shading shows battlefield land. Three layers are off when the map opens: the land Spain gave up in 1819 (green), the treaty line (pink dashes, in seven parts) and the Latin American nations, shown as blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824 and orange diamonds if later; the pop-up gives the exact date.
**Compelling question:** How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Where was the war fought? On the map: Open The War of 1812 bookmark. Click some diamonds in each group and read their pop-ups. Answer: In which three areas was most of the fighting?
2. The biggest battles On the map: Click the three biggest diamonds. Read where and when each battle was fought, and who won. Compare each battle's date with December 24, 1814, when the peace treaty was signed at Ghent. Answer: Where and when was each battle fought, and who won? Which big battle came after the peace treaty?
3. Florida and a new border On the map: Open The 1819 boundary bookmark. In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819. Click the green land and read its pop-up. Click each part of the pink dashed line and read its pop-up. Answer: What did the United States gain from Spain? Which rivers and lines of latitude and longitude does the new border follow?
4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine On the map: Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark. Turn on Latin American independence and US recognition. Click the blue circles and read each recognition date in the pop-up. Check each date against December 2, 1823 (blue only means recognized by 1824). Answer: Which nations had the United States recognized before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823? Why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out of the Americas?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about the War of 1812 and its results that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** impressment, blockade, Treaty of Ghent, cession, boundary, recognition, Monroe Doctrine, independence.
**Standards:** TX 8.5(E); TX 8.5(F); FL SS.8.A.4.1; C3 D2.His.1.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8.

**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
